I'd love to tell you all about the ways company's use your data for the better, and answer any questions you may have around Big, Cloud, or Relational data.

If you want to know how Data influences your day to day life(it does), ask me some specific questions and I'll tell you what I can.
IAMA Consultant in the Data Industry
Does data mining intrude on our privacy as we browse the Internet and/or use various social and photo sharing networks?

It does intrude on your privacy, but that is something that you trade off to use the sites that mine your data. This is also a question of your own personal tolerance, and the way you expect whatever entity collecting your information to handle your data.

My most recent/relevant example would be the Ashley Madison debacle. The users signed up for the website because they sought that specific service. They also signed away acknowledgements that AM would be collecting certain data. However; due to the sensitive nature of that data, and the users' implicit understanding that AM would protect that data, Ashley Madison should have done something, even basic masking to protect its user identities. Because they did not, they opened themselves up to a major intrusion of their users' privacy.

It's important to remember that many company's have good data practices, and do everything they can to ensure their data is safe. I'll reply again with a positive example of data mining below:

Certain companies have unprecedented access to large of amounts of user data. In my example, we'll look at positive outcomes for Geo-location data mining.

By mining Geo-location data, companies are able to see where you are every minute of the day. Though this isn't something you may want, it's here, it's happening, and it's being used. While your data yourself isn't necessarily important(unless you're a fugitive of some measure), when we look at large sets of data, companies can answer important business problems.

If I am a brick and mortar retailer, and want to build a new store, the first thing I'll do is buy a large amount of customer data in the area I'm looking to build a new store. I'll run a series of queries that plot out each customer in my demographics' (Maybe family of 4, elderly, 16-19, etc...) location at each point in the day, day after day. By doing this I'll be able to determine the best location to build my store. In this case, Data Mining increases both customer and retailer experience-- The retailer has put themselves in the best position to make money by putting themselves in proximity to their target audience, and the consumer gets easy access to a store they have a high likelihood of being interested in.

I can see why this would be a good thing for existing companies and those who are just starting, but I've read about several complaints about data mining intruding on privacy. Take for example, the complaints from some Google users and how they claim that Google is intruding on their Internet search data by suggesting products and sites, and even flat out shoving commercials in thier faces (like while watching a YouTube video) based off what they've searched for.

I've personally experienced this when I did an open search for Artificial Intelligence programs and DYI A.I. projects. Now, every time I go to YouTube or even any site or app associated with Google (such as Google Plus and Google Now), I get commercials and suggestions for A.I. computer programs, technology universities and even online social communities on Google Plus and Facebook.

It seems a bit aggressive and intrusive and makes me a bit more concerned of what I search for openly.

While the way you receive your advertisements may be aggressive(I think it is too), you have to understand that this is the next evolution in consumerism. Like it or not, if you want to have a smart phone with some apps on it, use websites to buy things, or in your example, use Google, you have to accept that you are no longer the only person who controls your personal information and identity.

Google became what it is because of its ability to position specific companies at the top of it's search list. Generation 1 Internet marketing...Wait for someone to search for you then be there. In Generation 2(now), those companies are there if you search for them(and they pay to be), and they are also in your face with direct ads if your data suggests you may be interested in what they have to offer.

Imagine that every time you get on the internet, your life becomes the Truman Show, and a large portion of the audience wants to predict what you need and provide it to you.
